No statewide civil death registration until 1913 — probate/estate files (1753-1970) are the primary substitute. A father's estate could be probated any time from his child's infancy to roughly 60 years after the child's birth; size the search window to the father's plausible lifespan, not the child's own.

collections.title: Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (synthetic test fixture)

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Death certificate found. Names Thomas Flynn as father. Informant was son-in-law James Brown.

- **1908 death certificate:** Names Thomas Flynn as father, but the informant was son-in-law James Brown — secondary information only.
- **Birthplace conflict (c_001):** Resolved in favour of Ireland.

**New plan — pl_003 (FAN-club approach, in execution order)**

| # | Plan item | Focus |
|---|-----------|-------|
| pli_006 | **Church records** — Schuylkill County parishes, 1845–1908 | Baptism sponsors, marriage witnesses, and Patrick's own children's baptisms; sponsors and witnesses are the core FAN leads |

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

Mode: create. Question q_001: "Where did Silas Bankston marry, circa 1828?"

Already in the tree:
- Birth about 1800, Feliciana Parish, Louisiana.
- Residence in 1820 in Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, from the 1820 census (S1).
- Silas has no FamilySearch ark, so I planned no hints-review item.

Plan pl_001, in execution order:
1. pli_001: marriage records, East Feliciana Parish, FamilySearch, 1824-1835. Collection 3000101 is name-searchable. Search Bankston and its variants.
2. pli_002: marriage records, West Feliciana Parish, FamilySearch, 1824-1835. Collection 3000102 is name-searchable. It is co-equal with pli_001, because the 1824 split means the record could be under either parish.
3. pli_003: 1830 census, both parishes, FamilySearch. It shows which parish Silas lived in and whether he had a wife by then. It is supporting evidence only.
4. pli_004: church marriage registers, both parishes, FamilySearch. It is the fallback for pli_001 and an independent source for the same event.
5. pli_005: probate and succession records, both parishes, 1828-1880, FamilySearch. It is the fallback for pli_001. It is also a relatives-and-associates item, since estates of Silas, his relatives or the bride's family may name a spouse and place. The window is set by Silas's likely lifespan.
6. pli_006: land and tax records, both parishes, 1820-1840, FamilySearch. They show where Silas lived relative to the split and who his neighbors were.

The plan has six items. The question asks for a marriage place, not a parentage, so no baptism or parents' marriage item is needed. The only validation warning was that the St. Francisville area wording on pli_004 is not inside the researched locality, Louisiana, United States. It is harmless.

Next step is search-records for the FamilySearch items, starting with pli_001 and pli_002.

---

The question is where Silas Bankston married around 1828. The only firm facts so far are that he was born around 1800 and was living in Feliciana Parish, Louisiana, in 1820. That parish was split into East and West Feliciana in 1824, and we don't know which half he lived in. So the plan searches the marriage registers of both parishes first, since both are name-searchable. After that it uses the 1830 census to see where he was living, then church marriage records. Estate files and land and tax records come last, to identify his wife or her family and narrow down the parish.

Next, the two parish marriage registers will be searched for Silas Bankston and spelling variants such as Bankson, for roughly 1824 to 1835.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

sources.citation: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, Recorder of Deeds, Deed Book 42, p. 118, Patrick Sheahan from James Kelly, 1875; FamilySearch digital images.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

entry.rationale: Tree facts: Residence 1870 Pennsylvania (log_001: farmer, household outside Schuylkill County); Residence 1882 Schuylkill County with Occupation Miner (log_002 directory). The 1880 census falls between them and lies inside the 1882 window, so it may show him already in Schuylkill County or still elsewhere, his occupation (farmer vs miner/laborer), birthplace, household and neighbours (FAN). Pins the move date and tests the mining premise directly.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

entry.rationale: Tree records Residence 1870 (Pennsylvania, no county), a log_001 1870 census farmer outside Schuylkill County, and Residence 1882 Schuylkill with Occupation Miner (log_002 directory). The 1880 census (United States Census, 1880, name-searchable) falls between: it shows whether he was still farming elsewhere or already in Schuylkill, bounding the move date and giving occupation and birthplace. Search Sheahan, Sheahan variants (Shehan, Sheehan, Shehan, Sheean).

loc_001: Catholic registers stay with the parish/Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county. The Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable; look for Michael's or his children's baptisms, marriage, or burial in a coal-town parish, which show where he lived and often a mining-patch parish. Use surname variants.

The 1900 census (name-searchable) records occupation, months unemployed, immigration year and household for Michael, showing whether mining remained his work and, via neighbors, the mining community. 1890 census is lost, so 1900 is the next window; reaches past 1882 to testify to the move.

Directly tests the hypothesis: colliery employment/payroll records and annual Pennsylvania mine inspectors' reports (company names, collieries) and city/county directories for 1883-1900 can place Michael at a specific colliery or mining company. Find holdings via the Pennsylvania State Archives or local historical societies; locate by catalog, not assumed.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: Follows pl_002 (1860 completed; tree holds 1850 and 1860 Thomas Flynn households with Patrick age 5 and 15, both Ireland-born, no relationships stated). Timeline t_001 has a high gap 1860-1908. United States Census, 1870 is name-searchable. Search Patrick Flynn b. ~1845 Ireland (tree and censuses say Ireland; death certificate says Pennsylvania, so do not filter on birthplace) with variants Flinn, Flin, Flynne, Fflynn; also search Thomas Flynn b. ~1818 Ireland in the same county to see if Patrick is still in his household. Patrick would be about 25, possibly newly married and in his own household.

United States Census, 1880 is name-searchable and is the first census stating relationship to head of household, which would turn the indirect 1850/1860 evidence into direct evidence if Patrick (about 35) or Thomas (about 62) is enumerated as son/father in a shared household, or if Thomas is listed in Patrick's home. It also gives parents' birthplaces. Use Flinn/Flin variants and search adjacent anthracite-region counties since miners moved between them.

United States Census, 1900 is name-searchable, records relationship, birth month/year, years married and parents' immigration data; Patrick (about 55) is alive then, and Thomas (about 82) may live in his household. The 1890 census is not planned because it was largely destroyed. Closes the later part of the 1860-1908 gap.

Fallback for the three FamilySearch census items if indexing misses Patrick (Irish surname variants are commonly mis-indexed). Ancestry has independent indexes of the same schedules; verify any hit against the image. Third-party coverage should be confirmed with the external collections lookup at search time.

Dedicated item for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818 Ireland) to Patrick's mother, and of Patrick's own marriage. Tree gives no mother or wife. The parents' marriage would confirm the couple as a unit and may name the mother's maiden name, though it likely occurred in Ireland before 1845 and may be unreachable here; it dates the union relative to Patrick's birth but does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. Patrick's marriage, probably 1865-1885 (his son-in-law informant implies daughters), may name his parents and place of origin. Loc_001 notes Pennsylvania civil registration began only in 1906, so rely on church marriage registers and county marriage records where they exist.

Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818) could die from 1860 into the early 1900s, so the window is set by his lifespan, not Patrick's. Loc_001 says the county Register of Wills holds wills and administrations from 1811 and these name heirs, which would be direct parentage evidence. Patrick's own estate (d. 1908) is also in scope as it may name siblings or mention his father. Check FamilySearch for browse-only image coverage first.

Patrick's own burial entry. Baptism is unlikely to be findable: tree and censuses place his birth ~1845 in Ireland, before any Pennsylvania parish register and in a place not yet known. Burial or cemetery entries and obituary (the Roman Catholic parish registers sit with the Diocese of Philadelphia/parish per loc_001, and cemetery and newspaper records) often state age, birthplace or parish of origin. The death certificate (pli_005) names Thomas as father but its informant was a son-in-law and it conflicts with the censuses on birthplace, so a church or cemetery record gives independent testimony.

FAN item. Review the neighbors on the 1870, 1880 and 1900 pages around Patrick's and Thomas's households, and trace Patrick's son-in-law James Brown (death certificate informant) and any Flynn households nearby with Irish birth, who may be Patrick's siblings, in-laws or townspeople from the same Irish origin. This may reveal siblings whose records name the same parents, and shows whether the Brown household sheltered Patrick or Thomas late in life.

Create a plan for searching the post-1860 federal censuses — 1870, 1880, and 1900 — to track Patrick Flynn as an adult and look for Thomas Flynn in the same household.

agent_returns.text:
**Mode:** Add-new. The earlier plan (pl_002) had every item finished, so I marked it completed and wrote a new active plan, pl_003. The question is q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?" The existing proof summary (ps_001) rates the conclusion only "probable". Patrick has no FamilySearch ark in the project tree, so I added no hints-review item.

**What the tree already records**
- Patrick (I1): born about 1845 in Ireland, from the 1850 census. Died 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, PA, per death certificate S3.
- Thomas Flynn (I2): born about 1818 in Ireland. He is linked as Patrick's father through the 1850 and 1860 censuses and the death certificate.
- The 1850 census shows Patrick, age 5, in Thomas's household. The 1860 census shows him at age 15. Neither census states relationships.
- The death certificate names Thomas as father. Its informant was Patrick's son-in-law, James Brown. It gives Pennsylvania as the birthplace, which conflicts with the censuses' Ireland.
- No mother or wife is recorded. Timeline t_001 flags a high-severity gap from 1860 to 1908.

**Plan pl_003, in execution order**
1. pli_006: 1870 census, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch. It is name-searchable, so I'd search Patrick and Thomas with Flinn and Flin variants, not filtering on birthplace.
2. pli_007: 1880 census, FamilySearch. It is the first census that states relationship to the head of household, so it could give direct evidence of parentage.
3. pli_008: 1900 census, FamilySearch. It gives relationship and years married, and Thomas (about 82) might be living in Patrick's household. I left out 1890 because that census was largely destroyed.
4. pli_009: 1870–1900 censuses on Ancestry, as a fallback for pli_006. It covers mis-indexed Irish surnames.
5. pli_010: Marriage records, 1865–1900, FamilySearch. This is the dedicated item for Thomas's marriage to Patrick's mother and for Patrick's own marriage. A marriage record would not by itself prove Patrick is their child.
6. pli_011: Probate in the county Register of Wills, 1860–1920. The window is sized to Thomas's possible lifespan. A will naming Patrick would be direct evidence. It also covers Patrick's own estate.
7. pli_012: Patrick's own burial entry, church, cemetery or obituary, 1908. A baptism is unlikely to exist because he was born in Ireland, before any Pennsylvania register. A burial entry may give his age or place of origin.
8. pli_013: FAN census review (relatives, neighbors, associates), 1870–1900. It looks at neighbors, James Brown, and nearby Irish-born Flynns who could be siblings.

I added no military or naming-customs wiki pages. They did not apply to a subject born in the British Isles with a simple surname. The 1870, 1880 and 1900 census collections are name-searchable on FamilySearch (collections 1438024, 1417683 and 1325221).

Hand-back: search-records for the FamilySearch items (pli_006 to pli_008, pli_010, pli_011, pli_013), and search-external-sites for the Ancestry fallback (pli_009). The burial item (pli_012) can go to either, depending on the repository.

---

This plan is for the question of who Patrick Flynn's parents were. We already have census records from 1850 and 1860 showing him as a boy in Thomas Flynn's household. We also have his 1908 death certificate, which names Thomas as his father. The next step is to look for him in the 1870, 1880 and 1900 censuses, since the 1880 and 1900 ones state how people in a household are related. After that come marriage records, Thomas's will or estate papers, Patrick's burial record, and neighbors and in-laws who might point to his Irish origins. If the censuses miss him because of misspelled names, a second index on Ancestry serves as a backup.

Next, the 1870, 1880 and 1900 census searches will run first, followed by the marriage, will, burial and neighbor searches.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

## Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Spain — 1835-1870

Before civil registration (1871) the parish books are the vital record. Santa María's books from 1837 are on FamilySearch, unindexed but full-text searchable; one births volume for 1841-1845 is name-indexed.

entry.rationale: Tree holds only her birth, about 1843 in Vélez-Málaga; no parent recorded. Civil registration began 1871 (loc_001), so the baptism is the primary record and normally names both parents and four grandparents. Spain, Baptisms, 1502-1940 and Spain, Catholic Church Records, 1307-2005 are name-searchable. Search María Josefa García Romero with variants (Josepha, Josefa, Maria Josepha; García/Garcia, Romero) and, per Spain Naming Customs, the child carries father's surname first, mother's second, so García = father's and Romero = mother's as a hypothesis only.

It does not alone prove María Josefa is their child; that needs the baptism or a household record. Use Spain, Marriages, 1565-1950 and Catholic Church Records; window set by parents' likely marrying ages. Check for earlier marriages of either parent since a remarriage could change surnames.

Her own marriage record or pre-marriage file typically states age, parents' names and home parish; useful if the baptism is not found or to corroborate it. Her marriage is unknown, so search Spain Marriages and Catholic Church Records by her name; also check Málaga municipal records. Civil marriage records exist from 1871.

Her own death or burial entry (Spain, Deaths, 1600-1920; parish burials; civil death register after 1871) usually names parents and age, an independent check on the baptism and a route if the baptism is misindexed. Window runs from birth to a plausible old-age death.

entry.jurisdiction: Santa María parish, Vélez-Málaga, Málaga, Spain
entry.rationale: FAN item: baptisms of siblings and her godparents' entries. Siblings baptized with the same García and Romero parents show the family unit and help distinguish her from other María Josefa García entries; godparents (often kin) may appear in the parents' marriage and in her own marriage as witnesses. Window spans the parents' likely childbearing years.

Spain, Málaga, Municipal Records, 1760-1956 is name-searchable and may hold censuses/padrones or civil entries placing María Josefa in a household with parents; use to link her to the parents found in the baptism. Also a wider net if the family moved within the province.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1838-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Tree holds only Bridget (b. ~1838 Ireland) with John Doyle and daughter Ellen; log_002 (1900 census) says Bridget bore 9 children, 2 living, so ~7 died young or left. Households of John and Bridget Doyle in the 1860 and 1870 United States Census (both name-searchable) should list children by name and age, including ones who died before 1879. Search Doyle, Doyel, Doyl and Halloran/Holloran/Halleran variants; the tree's Ellen marriage (log_003, 1865-1875) suggests Ellen may be older than Bridget's stated birth year, so check ages and household composition rather than assuming all children are Bridget's.

The 1880 census (name-searchable) records relationship to head, so it can show Doyle children as stepchildren in Martin Kearney's household (Bridget m. Kearney 1879, log_001) or in separate households. Also reveals if John Doyle was already dead.

loc_001: statewide birth registration began only in 1906 and Catholic registers (Archdiocese of Philadelphia) are held by parish, so baptisms are the main source for births 1855-1879. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable; search baptisms with parents John Doyle and Bridget Halloran (and variants), capturing sponsors as FAN names.

Fallback if the name search misses: loc_001 notes coal-region church films are browse-only image groups. Image group 007936751 (Schuylkill church records 1842-1895) is browse-only (personCount 0, 0% record-searchable); browse Catholic parish baptism pages image by image for Doyle entries.

Burial entries for John Doyle (died before Bridget's 1879 remarriage) and for infant Doyle children: Doyle child burials explain the ~7 deaths and name parents or ages. Search the name-searchable church collection for burials, then cemetery records. Death predates 1906 civil registration (loc_001).

loc_001: Register of Wills records from 1811 name heirs. Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0) as is image group 007936749 (1851-1930, 0% record-searchable). Browse for an estate or administration of John Doyle (spouse and children as heirs) and later Bridget's/Martin Kearney's estate. Window runs to 1930 because the creators (John, then Bridget) could die long after the children's births.

Dedicated search for the marriage of John Doyle and Bridget Halloran to each other: confirms the couple, fixes the start of the children's window and may name witnesses. Use Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 (both name-searchable) plus church marriage entries; Irish origin means the marriage may predate arrival, so note it may be in Ireland.

FAN/sibling item: marriages of other Doyle children list parents as John Doyle and Bridget Halloran, as Ellen's did (log_003). Search Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 (name-searchable) by parent names, and browse image group 007936753 (Schuylkill marriage records 1870-1910, browse-only, personCount 0). Witnesses and bondsmen may be siblings.

The 1900 Kearney household (log_002) shows 2 children living; identify the second survivor besides Ellen by checking 1900 and 1910 censuses (name-searchable) for Ellen's household and Bridget/Martin Kearney's, including boarders or neighbors who may be a Doyle child.

Bridget Kearney's (and Martin Kearney's) death certificate if after 1906 (Pennsylvania, Death Certificates 1906-1968, name-searchable) names informant and parents; plus burial and obituary naming surviving children. Also death certificates of Doyle siblings listing mother Bridget.
